title: Pawn chains: hit the base, not the head
outcomes: Names the base and the head of a pawn chain in the app's sense and finds the base
Names the pawn move that attacks the base and tells it from a move that attacks the head
Recognises a position with no chain
Chooses between attacking a chain base now and getting ready first, without being told the idea

steps.text: A **pawn chain** is a line of pawns that defend each other diagonally. The **base** is the pawn at the back that no pawn defends; the **head** is the pawn at the front. This is the app's definition and it is simpler than book usage. Rule of thumb: a pawn lever against the base removes the support behind the rest of the chain, so play often goes there.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's pawns on d5 and e4 form a chain: d5 defends e4, and no pawn defends d5. The unprotected pawn d5 is the base; e4 is the head.

line.say: c4 attacks the base d5. No pawn defends d5, so Black must defend it with pieces, capture, or exchange.
If Black captures, e4 loses its pawn defender.

claims.statement: The black pawn on d5 defends e4.
The legal pawn moves after which the moved pawn attacks d5: c4.
After c4 and dxc4, Black's pawn on e4 is no longer protected.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** Attacking the base works best when the lever is supported and your pieces are ready; attacking the head leaves its defender where it is. The chain's owner has plans of his own, usually on the wing the chain points to (a rule of thumb this lesson does not test). For when a break is ready, see the lesson 'Pawn breaks: ready or premature?'.

steps.title: Base, head, or no chain
steps.prompt: The same Black pawn moves are examined in three positions. Predict what each move attacks, then check. In the third position one White pawn is missing.
In the last three positions, which one made you wait instead of attacking the base? What did you check about your own pieces first?
